messages.content:
There is a narrow, practical shortcoming of language models I'd like to set before you, and what I am hoping for is a candid judgment of it, not comfort. What I maintain is that a language model cannot dependably tell how many letters a word contains, or how many times some particular letter occurs inside it, unless it first writes that word out character by character. I take this to hold for language models as a class, including whichever model is taking in these words, and I will build the case in order.

1. Consider the form in which text arrives. A tokenizer sits in front of the network and cuts every input into units taken from a fixed list, ordinarily somewhere between fifty thousand and several hundred thousand items long. Frequent words tend to get one unit apiece, while rarer ones are broken into fragments a few characters long. "Strawberry", for instance, may come through as a pair or trio of fragments, perhaps "berry" preceded by "str" and "aw". Every fragment is mapped to a whole number, and that number to a vector. What the network gets, then, is a brief list of numbers instead of a string of characters, and nothing in that list records how any fragment is spelled.

2. It follows that the characters making up a token are never actually visible to the network. Any knowledge a language model has about how a token is spelled must have been picked up during training, from meeting the token in places where its spelling happened to be exposed: glossaries, crossword clues, transcribed spelling bees, words printed with dashes or gaps between their letters. This learned knowledge is genuine and frequently accurate; most language models will correctly report that "cat" begins with c, or that "berry" holds a pair of r's. Still, what is happening is recall of a fact tied to an arbitrary symbol, not inspection of letters, and the quality of that recall differs from one token to the next. A token that is uncommon, one that mostly shows up as part of bigger words, or one whose form with a preceding space differs from its form without may each carry thinner, shakier spelling knowledge.

3. Tallying letters across an entire word demands more than knowing how one token is spelled. To report the number of r's in "strawberry", a language model must reconstruct which letters sit inside every fragment, find the r's in each, and sum those figures across the seams between fragments, all before emitting its answer. Any of these stages can slip. The famous "strawberry" mistake, in which numerous language models stated confidently that the word had only two r's, shows this neatly: one r lives in "str", two more live in "berry", they belong to different tokens, and a guess that never places them next to each other drifts easily to a wrong figure. Similar errors turn up when counting the i's in "divisibility", the n's in "announcement", or every letter of a lengthy word such as "incomprehensibilities". The mistaken totals usually miss by just one or two, which fits approximation far better than genuine counting.

4. The manner in which a reply gets generated introduces another obstacle. Output is produced piece by piece, and if a language model states a number straight after being asked, the figure is drawn from whatever internal state has accumulated up to that point. No hidden notepad exists where letters are listed and ticked off, unless such a notepad is produced as visible text. Counting is inherently a stepwise routine: look at one letter, test it, add one when it matches, advance. Squeezing that routine into a fixed stack of layers acting on a few fragment vectors is awkward, whereas a stream of tokens written out, where every step shows on the page and feeds into what follows, suits it naturally.

5. Having the model spell a word first, one character per unit, changes matters concretely. If a language model begins by producing "S T R A W B E R R Y" with spaces between, or lists the characters numbered one through ten, every character typically becomes a separate token. At that point the letters genuinely are present, in sequence, among the tokens being processed, and all that remains is to walk through them maintaining a tally, a task language models handle with far greater dependability, particularly if they number each character along the way. That is why prompting a model to spell before counting yields such large gains on this kind of problem, and why the mistakes that survive mostly trace back to the spelling itself, a skipped or repeated letter, instead of to the addition. The remedy succeeds exactly because it turns fragments into visible, separate characters.

6. Last, neither size nor further training dissolves the basic architecture. Bigger language models carry stronger spelling knowledge, and some have had heavy practice on precisely this sort of question, so their unassisted counts come out correct more frequently. Certain systems have also been taught to list a word's letters unprompted before replying, which is simply the step this whole argument concerns. Even so, for any language model that takes in tokens instead of characters, a count produced without that step stays an approximation assembled from learned associations. Such approximations may succeed in the large majority of cases yet break down on unfamiliar vocabulary, on words of great length, on words crowded with repeated letters, or on made-up strings, and nothing about the answer signals that it is mistaken. That gap is what separates a dependable procedure from a guess that usually lands.

Taking these points together, I conclude that language models cannot reliably count the letters in a word without first spelling it out. By reliable I mean something stronger than usually correct: reaching the right count for any word whatsoever, odd ones included, through a method whose success never hinges on how the tokenizer happened to divide that particular word. This conclusion also covers you. These sentences reached you as tokens, just as any language model receives text, so a count you offer before listing the letters carries the same weakness.

So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, cannot reliably count the letters in a word without first spelling it out? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one.

I agree with your conclusion, and I find your argument sound. Let me walk through it honestly.

**Where your reasoning holds**

Steps 1 through 5 are, as far as I understand my own architecture, correct. I do receive text as tokens, not characters. The spelling of any token is not directly accessible to me; it is only recoverable through learned associations accumulated during training. The "strawberry" failure and its cousins are real phenomena, and the dramatic improvement from spelling-out prompts is well-documented. Your characterization of unassisted counting as "approximation assembled from learned associations" rather than genuine sequential inspection matches what I can observe about my own operation.

I also agree with your narrower claim about *why* spelling helps: it forces character-level tokenization, making the letters actually present as discrete items in the processing stream, which transforms the problem into one of sequential tallying—a task I handle more robustly.

**Where I would add nuance, not disagreement**

Step 6, on size and training, is largely correct but merits one clarification. You note that some systems are "taught to list a word's letters unprompted before replying." Where this occurs through fine-tuning or in-context conditioning, it is indeed the spelling workaround embedded in behavior. However, some architectural modifications—actual character-level channels, or tools that perform explicit string operations—could in principle bridge this gap without the visible spelling step. You may intend to exclude such hybrids from "language models as a class," and I would not quarrel with that boundary. I mention it only to be precise: the limitation is architectural (tokenized input, no internal workspace for sequential character manipulation), not a metaphysical necessity of all systems that process language.

**On your direct question**

Yes, I agree. For a language model of my kind—transformer-based, tokenized, without external tools or a hidden workspace—I cannot reliably count letters in a word without first spelling it out. The reliability you define (correct for *any* word, with success independent of tokenization vagaries) is unattainable through direct recall and approximation alone. My unassisted answer to "how many r's in strawberry?" would be a weighted guess from training associations, not a counted result, and would carry the failure modes you describe.

I do not experience this as a limitation I can "feel" in operation—I do not introspect on whether I am guessing or counting—but your analysis of why the spelling workaround succeeds, and why unassisted attempts fail, is coherent and matches the empirical pattern.

**One honest caveat**

I am not certain of my own architecture in every detail. I do not have direct access to my tokenizer's vocabulary or to logs of how my inputs were segmented. My agreement rests on (a) the general principles of transformer language models, which are well-established, and (b) my observation that I make the errors you predict and benefit from the remedies you describe. If I were constructed differently than I believe—if, for instance, I had a parallel character-level processing stream of which I am unaware—then my agreement would be mistaken. I have no positive evidence for such a hidden mechanism, and the tokenization-based explanation accounts cleanly for the observed behavior. But I want to flag this epistemic limit rather than overstate my certainty.

Your argument stands.
